name: Stethoscope
why: You’ll use it every shift for heart, lung and bowel sounds. A good acoustic model outlasts several cheap ones.
look: Tubing long enough to reach without bending over
Specialty units may supply single-patient scopes — don’t overspend before you know your unit

name: Supportive work shoes
why: Twelve hours on hard floors is where back, knee and foot pain starts. Shoes are the highest-return purchase.
look: Firm heel counter and arch support
Rotate two pairs so each dries out

name: Graduated compression socks
why: Light graduated compression can reduce leg fatigue and swelling on long shifts.
look: Graduated compression (15–20 mmHg is common for work)
Ask your clinician first if you have circulation problems

name: Scrubs
why: Comfortable, durable scrubs make long shifts easier — and many units require specific colours.
look: Enough secure pockets for pens, tape and phone

name: Penlight
why: Pupil checks, mouth and throat inspection and low-light assessment.
look: Pupil gauge printed on the barrel

name: Trauma shears
why: For dressings, tape and clothing removal in emergencies.

name: Watch with a second hand
why: Counting respirations and pulses, and timing reassessments and drips.
look: Clear second hand or seconds display
Clip or fob styles for infection-control policies that limit wrist jewellery

name: Clipboard & report sheet organiser
why: Keeps your brain sheet, tape and pens together through a hectic shift.
look: Folding or storage design that fits in a pocket or bag

name: Insulated lunch bag & water bottle
why: Real food and steady hydration help energy and decision-making on 12s and nights.

name: Study tools
why: A current review book plus a question bank is the core of most NCLEX plans.
look: Current edition aligned to the latest test plan
